audio_script: A ball drops from a shelf. Its speed grows, but where did that motion come from? Choose the ball and the Earth as one system. At the top, the system has gravitational potential energy, equal to mass times gravity times height. As the ball falls, its height decreases, so that stored energy goes down. Gravity speeds the ball up, increasing its kinetic energy, which is one half mass times velocity squared. If we ignore air resistance, the decrease in potential energy equals the increase in kinetic energy. For a two kilogram object dropping five meters near the Earth's surface, the change in potential energy is about ninety-eight point one joules. This animation is not a stylized fall. It is the actual solution of the equation of motion. Gravity is constant, so the velocity grows linearly with time, and the position changes quadratically. Watch the trail accelerate downward. The readout shows time, position, and speed at every frame, computed by numerical integration of Newton's second law. Now look at the equations. Potential energy is mass times gravity times height. Kinetic energy is one half mass times velocity squared. Their sum does not change. That is the content of the law. But conservation is only true after you decide what is inside the system. Include the air, and some of the energy becomes heat. Include the Earth, and potential energy is well defined. Exclude either, and the ledger no longer balances. This is why every energy problem begins with the same question: what is the system? Name it, name the assumptions, then follow every transfer across the boundary.

audio_script: A police officer stops a driver. You were going sixty miles an hour, he says. She objects. I have only been driving for seven minutes. The officer is not claiming she covered sixty miles. He is claiming that if she kept going at that rate, she would. That is the idea of instantaneous speed. Measure where the car is at one time, then at a slightly later time. Divide the change in position by the change in time. That is average speed, and it depends on which two times you pick. Now shrink the interval. The average settles toward a limit. That limit is the instantaneous speed. On the graph, the yellow secant line joins two measured points on the curve. As the interval shrinks, the secant rotates toward the green tangent at the later point. The tangent's slope is the speed at that instant. For this demonstration, position goes as one half a t squared, with acceleration equal to one. At two point four seconds, the exact speed is two point four meters per second. Not the average over any interval, but the exact value at that instant. Newton and Leibniz discovered this independently in the same decade, working on the same problem, which was motion. Every local rate in physics is a derivative. Temperature change per second. Current through a wire. Population growth. Calculus begins with the question of instantaneous change.

audio_script: A puck sliding on frictionless ice keeps moving after the push ends. Newton's first law says an object keeps constant velocity when the net external force is zero. A net force changes velocity. The change per unit time is acceleration. Newton's second law writes this as the net force equals mass times acceleration. But the law is not a definition. If it were, physics would be empty. The law is a program for studying nature. It says that when you compute mass times acceleration and call the result force, you will find that forces are simple. Now look at a projectile. On the right, a ball is launched at eight meters per second at fifty-five degrees. Its path is a parabola. Why? Because two independent things happen at once. Horizontally, no force, so constant velocity. Vertically, constant gravity, so constant acceleration. On the left, the initial velocity is decomposed into its horizontal and vertical components. The vertical component is eight times sine of fifty-five degrees, about six point five five. The horizontal component is eight times cosine of fifty-five degrees, about four point five nine. Combining them produces the parabola on the right. The horizontal velocity never changes. The vertical velocity shrinks, reverses at the apex, and grows again downward. This is why the path is symmetric. Nothing is pulling the ball forward. Nothing is slowing its horizontal motion.

audio_script: Two carts roll toward each other. The cart on the left has mass two, moving at zero point nine meters per second to the right. The cart on the right has mass one, moving at zero point six meters per second to the left. Total momentum before the collision is two times zero point nine plus one times negative zero point six, which equals one point two kilogram meters per second. During the brief collision, the carts exert equal and opposite forces on one another. Those forces act for the same time, so the impulses are equal and opposite. One cart's gain is the other's loss. After the collision, momentum conservation and the elastic collision condition give both final velocities. The final velocity of the heavy cart is negative zero point one. The final velocity of the light cart is one point four. Check the total momentum: two times negative zero point one plus one times one point four, which is one point two. Unchanged. Check the total kinetic energy: before it was zero point nine nine joules, after it is also zero point nine nine. The collision is elastic. The animation shows exactly this collision, computed from the elastic formulas. Choose your system first. Then compare momentum before and after. The rule is universal.

audio_script: A solid disk and a thin rod. Same mass of two kilograms. Same torque of zero point five newton meters applied to each. The disk spins up quickly. The rod turns slowly. Why? Because mass alone does not determine how a body resists turning. What matters is how far the mass sits from the axis. For a uniform disk about its center, the moment of inertia is one half mass times radius squared. For a disk of mass two and radius zero point nine, that is zero point eight one kilogram meter squared. For a rod pivoted at one end, the moment of inertia is one third mass times length squared. For a rod of mass two and length two point two, that is three point two three kilogram meter squared. The same torque produces less angular acceleration when the inertia is larger. The disk's angular acceleration is zero point six two radians per second squared. The rod's is zero point one six. That is a ratio of about four to one. Watch the animation. Same torque, dramatically different response. This is why a door handle is placed far from the hinge. This is why a long pendulum swings slower than a short one. The mass has not changed. Only the arrangement has.

audio_script: A satellite is not beyond gravity. It is falling toward the Earth all the time. So why does it not hit the ground? Because it also has sideways velocity. As gravity bends its path inward, the satellite moves forward enough that the curved Earth falls away beneath it. An orbit is a continuous fall that keeps missing. The animation on the left is not a pre-drawn ellipse. It is the numerical solution of Newton's law of gravitation, with a force that falls off as one over r squared. Set the orbital radius to two and the gravitational parameter mu to eighteen. The circular speed is the square root of eighteen over two, which is three. The satellite is launched at exactly that speed, perpendicular to the radius. The result is a circular orbit with period about four point one nine seconds. On the right, the graph shows the inverse-square law: the force at radius one is one, at radius two is one quarter, at radius three is one ninth. Doubling the distance reduces the force by a factor of four. Notice that the satellite's mass drops out of the circular speed formula. A pebble and a space station at the same radius would follow the same path. That is a deep hint about gravity. Real orbits also experience drag and tides. But the geometric picture survives: continuous inward acceleration plus sideways velocity.

audio_script: Pull a mass on a spring and let it go. It bounces up and down. Pull it twice as far, and it still takes the same time to return. This is strange. You would expect a bigger displacement to take longer. But it does not. Why? Because the restoring force grows with the displacement. Twice as far means twice the force. Twice the force means twice the acceleration. Twice the acceleration covers twice the distance in the same time. The time pattern is fixed by the system, not the amplitude. On the left, the spring and mass are integrated numerically. The mass has mass one and the spring has stiffness four, so the natural frequency is the square root of four over one, which equals two radians per second. That matches the graph on the right, which plots a cosine with angular frequency two. Watch the mass complete one cycle in three point one four seconds. A stiffer spring oscillates faster. A heavier mass oscillates slower. The same cosine appears in electrical circuits, molecular vibrations, small-angle pendulums, and light emitted by atoms. Any system whose restoring force is proportional to displacement obeys this equation. Its mathematics seeds quantum mechanics.

audio_script: When a force pushes an object, the object gains kinetic energy. If the force is constant, work equals force times distance. But what if the force varies? Imagine stretching a spring. As you pull, the force grows. Near the start, little force. Near the end, a lot. Break the displacement into small steps. Over each step, the force is roughly constant. Multiply the local force by the step size. Add all the products together. That sum is the work. On the left, ten rectangles approximate the area under the curve of a spring with stiffness four. On the right, the same curve with the exact area shaded. Both panels plot the same function. The rectangles use midpoints, so the approximation is accurate to within a few percent. For a spring, the exact area is one half k L squared, where L is the total stretch. With stiffness four and stretch one point five, that is four point five joules. This is the elastic potential energy. It matches the kinetic energy gained by the spring when released. Work and energy are two views of the same physics. Derivatives compute force from energy. question_text: A car travels 60 km in the first hour and 90 km in the next two hours. What is its average speed over the whole journey?

column18: A car travels sixty kilometers in the first hour and ninety kilometers in the next two hours. What is its average speed over the whole journey? The average speed is the total distance divided by the total time. Total distance is sixty plus ninety, one hundred fifty kilometers. Total time is one plus two, three hours. One hundred fifty divided by three is fifty kilometers per hour. Option A. Notice that we do not simply average the two speeds. If we did, we would get seventy-five kilometers per hour, which is wrong. The car went at different speeds for different amounts of time, so we must weight by time. Whenever you see the phrase average speed, remember: total distance over total time.
